question: How long does God's anger last?
summary: The Bible gives at least four mutually incompatible answers about the duration of God's anger. Judith 8:15 says God doesn't get angry at all. Psalm 30:5 says His anger lasts only a moment. Numbers 32:13, Psalm 103:9, Jeremiah 3:12, and Micah 7:18 say His anger doesn't last forever (but sometimes for forty years). Jeremiah 17:4, Malachi 1:4, and Matthew 25:41-46 say His anger and punishment burn forever.

reconcile.connective: Defenders resolve the tension by the object of the anger: God's wrath toward his own repentant people is momentary, while toward the impenitent it abides.

discrepancy.connective: Robert G. Ingersoll presses the sharpest form of the objection, arguing that in the Old Testament 'the vengeance of Jehovah stopped at the tomb' and that it was the New Testament that newly introduced the doctrine of eternal pain — so the duration of divine wrath is not one consistent teaching but escalates across the canon.

pd_work.resource: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible (1706-14), on Micah 7:18
pd_work.author: Matthew Henry
pd_work.note: Henry treats this exact tension on Micah 7:18, distinguishing that God 'will not retain his anger for ever' toward the remnant of his heritage while 'against those that are not of the remnant of his heritage, that are unpardoned, he will keep his anger for ever' — the object-based harmonization keyed to the duration-of-anger question.

excerpts.attribution: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63)
excerpts.excerpt_text: neither will he keep his anger for ever; though he does with the wicked, yet not with his own people; that endures but for a moment, and is rather seeming than real
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly harmonizes both poles of the contradiction: anger 'for ever' is true of the wicked (Jer 17:4 / Mal 1:4 / Matt 25 type), while toward 'his own people' it endures 'but for a moment' (Ps 30:5 / Ps 103:9). The duration depends on the object, not a flat self-contradiction.

He will not always chide,.... He sometimes does chide his children, though never but when they have done a fault; always for their sins, in order to bring them to a sense and acknowledgment of them, and to depart from them; not for chiding sake, as some parents, to gratify their passion and ill humour, who correct for their own pleasure; but the Lord chides and corrects for the profit of his children, that they may be partakers of his holiness; he ever does it for their good, but he will not always chide, or continue it ever: or "he will not always contend" (e), strive with them, litigate a point with them, hold out a controversy, not being able to stand before him; he knows their frame, their weakness, and frailty; see Isa 57:16,
neither will he keep his anger for ever; though he does with the wicked, yet not with his own people; that endures but for a moment, and is rather seeming than real; and what does appear is soon turned away; he does not retain it long, he is quickly pacified towards them for all they have done, and smiles again upon them, Mic 7:18.
(e) "contendet", Pagninus, Montanus; "litigat", Junius & Tremellius, Piscator; "litigabit", Vatablus, Gejerus, Michaelis.
